ippuku — a bowl of tea — a tea break; a small pause that makes room for reflection
kaiseki — the seasonal multi-course meal served before a formal tea ceremony
kyuusu — Japanese teapot — a side-handled clay pot with a built-in strainer, for green tea
sadou — the Way of Tea — the tea ceremony as a spiritual and aesthetic practice rooted in Zen
chagama — tea kettle — the iron kettle that boils water in the tea room
chashi — tea master — an expert who evaluates, blends and refines tea leaves
chashaku — tea scoop — the bamboo scoop that measures matcha powder
chasen — bamboo whisk — 80–120 fine tines that whisk matcha into a frothy suspension
chasen naoshi — whisk stand — a ceramic rest that holds a chasen in shape after use
chanoyu — hot water for tea — a synonym for chadō; the ritual of preparing and serving matcha
chabashira — tea pillar — a stem standing upright in the cup; a rare sign of good luck
chawan — tea bowl — the bowl matcha is whisked and drunk from; usually handmade and seasonal
teishu — host — the tea master who prepares and serves the tea in a ceremony
natsume — matcha caddy — a lidded container for matcha, named for its jujube-like shape
mizusashi — water jar — the lidded container of fresh water used through a tea ceremony
asamushicha — light-steamed tea — steamed only 10–30 seconds; clear golden liquor and bright astringency
aracha — coarse tea — leaf that has been dried but not yet sorted or refined
ichoucha — withered tea — green tea slightly withered to draw out a floral aroma
kamairicha — pan-fired tea — leaf heated in a pan instead of steamed; made in southern Japan
kuradashicha — storehouse tea — spring sencha aged in storage; rounder and richer in umami
chuumushicha — mid-steamed tea — steamed 30–60 seconds; balanced between asamushi and fukamushi
temomicha — hand-rolled tea — a rare, labour-intensive tea rolled leaf by leaf by hand
fukamushicha — deep-steamed tea — steamed 1–3 minutes; vivid green, mellow, less astringent
futsuumushi — ordinary steaming — the standard steaming time; see chumushicha
ichigo ichie — one time, one meeting — every encounter is unique and unrepeatable
omotenashi — hospitality — sincere, selfless service that anticipates the guest's needs
kintsugi — golden joinery — repairing broken ceramics with gold-dusted lacquer, celebrating the crack
wakei seijaku — harmony, respect, purity, tranquillity — the four principles at the root of chadō
wabi sabi — wabi-sabi — the beauty of imperfection, impermanence and simplicity
amami — sweetness — the natural sweetness of amino acids (esp. L-theanine), strongest in shaded teas
umami — the savoury, broth-like taste that comes from L-theanine and amino acids
shibumi — astringency — the refined, delicate sharpness that gives good tea depth and structure
Awa bancha — lightly fermented bancha from Tokushima, with a lactic tang
ishizuchi kurocha — Stone Hammer black tea — a post-fermented folk tea from Mt. Ishizuchi, Ehime
usucha — thin tea — the usual ceremonial matcha, about 2 g whisked light and frothy
kabusecha — shaded tea — covered 7–14 days before harvest; more umami and sweetness, less bitterness
karigane — stem tea from gyokuro or high-grade sencha; a Kansai term
kancha — cold tea — a rare tea picked in midwinter (Dec–Feb); mellow with soft astringency
kyoubancha — Kyoto bancha — bancha steamed, dried and then roasted; smoky in character
gyokushin — leaf tips sifted out of unrefined gyokuro; a Kyoto term
gyokuro — jade dew — top-grade tea shaded some three weeks before harvest; sweet, deeply umami
kukicha — stem tea — made from the stalks and stems of young leaf; light, creamy, naturally sweet
genmaicha — brown rice tea — green tea blended with toasted rice; nutty and toasty
koicha — thick tea — ceremonial matcha, about 4 g with little water; syrupy and bold
konacha — powder tea — the fine bits left from making sencha or gyokuro; brisk, bold, quick to brew
goishicha — Japan's only truly fermented tea, from Kochi; named after the game of go
sanpincha — Okinawan jasmine tea, made from Chinese oolong and jasmine flowers
shira-ore — another name for kukicha (stem tea)
shincha — new tea — the first flush of early spring (April–May); aromatic, sweet and rich
sencha — steamed, rolled and dried leaf; the green tea drunk most in Japan
tamacha — round tea — sencha rolled into balls instead of needles
tamaryokucha — ball green tea — a sencha that skips the final needle-rolling step
tencha — shaded leaf dried without rolling; the raw material for matcha
toubancha — tea that skips steaming or pan-firing to raise its polysaccharides
Tosa bancha — a bancha from Tosa, Kochi Prefecture
nihoncha — Japanese tea — the traditional teas of Japan, not its black or oolong teas
bancha — ordinary tea — coarse late-grown leaf; high in catechins, so healthy but more bitter
bukubukucha — Okinawan tea whisked into a mountain of foam and eaten with red rice
houjicha — roasted tea — pan-roasted at high heat; toasty and nutty, low in bitterness and caffeine
boucha — stick tea — another name for roasted kukicha (stem tea)
matcha — finely ground powder of shade-grown tencha leaf, whisked rather than steeped
Mimasaka bancha — lightly fermented tea from Okayama, boiled in an iron pan
mecha — bud tea — the youngest tips and buds sorted out of high-grade tea; concentrated umami
ryokucha — green tea — the general term for Japan's unfermented teas
wakoucha — Japanese black tea — milder, smoother and sweeter than imported black teas
batabatacha — a post-fermented tea from Toyama, drunk whisked
botebotecha — whisked tea of Shimane's Edo-period steel workers
